title: Find your sea legs
intro: Welcome aboard. tmux keeps your terminal workspace alive, even when you leave. Let's get comfortable before we set sail.
concept: A session is your workspace. Windows are tabs inside it. Panes divide a window into multiple terminals. The terminal on the right is real — click it before using shortcuts.
steps: Click Connect terminal below the practice area. You're in a window called practice. Run pwd to see where you are.
Try the window chooser, then press Escape to return. Open key-binding help and press q to leave it.
When you're comfortable, click Check my work. This first mission is self-assessed.
tip: The prefix is a sequence: hold Ctrl and press b, release BOTH, then press the next key. Don't hold Ctrl for the second key.
checkpoint: Connect to your practice session and try the shortcuts.

title: Open a new horizon
intro: One window for your code, another for your server, another for notes. Give each task a little room.
concept: Each new tmux window has its own shell. Switching windows doesn't stop anything running in the others.
steps: With the terminal focused, create a new window.
Rename the new window to notes. At tmux's prompt, press Ctrl-u to clear the old name, type notes, then press Enter.
Run echo "Ahoy, Captain Pane!" in your new shell.
tip: Don't rename practice — we'll use it as your home port for later missions.

title: Chart your workspace
intro: A good workspace has names you can recognize and routes you can navigate without thinking.
concept: The status bar lists your windows. You can cycle through them, choose one from a list, or jump back to the last one.
steps: Select notes using the window chooser.
Rename notes to journal. At the rename prompt, use Ctrl-u to clear the old name, then type journal and press Enter.
Try next, previous, and last-window shortcuts. End in whichever window you like.
tip: A checkpoint checks the result, not every keystroke. Take your time exploring the shortcuts.
checkpoint: journal exists and notes no longer exists.

title: Divide and conquer
intro: Two views, one window. Keep a command running on one side while you work on the other.
concept: Panes share a window, but each has its own terminal. Zoom temporarily gives one pane the full window without closing the others.
steps: Use the window chooser to select practice.
Split it into at least two panes. Try moving focus and running pwd in each.
Try zooming a pane, unzooming it, and cycling through layouts.
tip: If tmux says the pane is too small, enlarge the app window and try again. % usually requires Shift-5 on a US keyboard.
checkpoint: practice contains at least two panes.

title: Give every pane a berth
intro: Three terminals do not have to mean a cramped deck. Let tmux arrange them for you.
concept: Layouts rearrange existing panes without restarting their shells. even-horizontal gives each pane a side-by-side column; even-vertical stacks them.
steps: Select practice. If needed, use Ctrl-b % until it contains exactly three panes. Unzoom with Ctrl-b z if a single pane fills the window.
Open the tmux command prompt with Ctrl-b :, type select-layout even-horizontal, and press Enter. This is a tmux command, not a shell command.
Try cycling layouts with Ctrl-b Space, then return to even-horizontal using the command prompt before checking.
tip: If the terminal feels cramped, enlarge the app or drag its edge. Layout changes preserve each shell and its running commands.
checkpoint: practice has at least three unzoomed panes in equal-width, side-by-side columns.

title: Make room for the big job
intro: A log viewer needs less room than your editor. Give the task that matters a little more space.
concept: You can resize a pane without changing the layout of your whole workspace. Resize commands use terminal cells, not pixels.
steps: Select practice and keep the three side-by-side panes from the previous mission. Select the leftmost pane with Ctrl-b Left (repeat as needed).
Press Ctrl-b : and enter resize-pane -R 10 to grow this pane to the right by ten columns.
Try resize-pane -L 5 to take back five columns, then resize-pane -R 10 again. Leave the columns noticeably unequal before checking.
keys: Focus the pane to the left
tip: Choose the leftmost pane so there is a neighbor to its right. If there is not enough space, enlarge the app before resizing.
checkpoint: practice has at least three unzoomed side-by-side panes, with column widths differing by at least eight cells.

title: Bring one task into focus
intro: Sometimes one task deserves the whole screen. Zoom in without closing the rest of your workspace.
concept: Zoom changes what you see, not how many panes exist. Other shells keep running while they are hidden. A Z in tmux’s status bar marks a zoomed window.
steps: Select a pane in practice. Keep at least two panes in that window.
Press Ctrl-b z to zoom the selected pane. Press it again to see your original layout return.
Zoom once more and leave it zoomed while you click Check my work. The next mission starts by unzooming.
tip: A zoomed pane is not a new window. Do not type exit to leave zoom: that would close the shell.
checkpoint: practice has multiple panes and is currently zoomed.

title: Move a task to a new berth
intro: Your workspace can evolve with your work. Move a running shell between windows instead of starting over.
concept: join-pane relocates a pane, keeping its shell and programs alive. Its -t argument names the destination window; -h places the moved pane beside an existing pane.
steps: Select practice and unzoom with Ctrl-b z. Keep at least two panes in practice.
Make sure journal exists using Ctrl-b w. If it is missing (for example, after finishing the original course), create a window with Ctrl-b c, rename it journal with Ctrl-b , and return to practice.
In a practice pane, run export MOVED_ABOARD=ahoy. Then open Ctrl-b : and enter join-pane -h -t practice:journal.
In the moved shell, run echo $MOVED_ABOARD. It should still say ahoy. Leave journal with at least two panes and keep practice alive.
tip: Enter join-pane at the tmux command prompt, not at your shell prompt. The following cleanup missions will close the extra practice panes and retire journal.
checkpoint: journal contains at least two panes, and practice still has a running pane.

title: Keep a tidy deck
intro: Time to tidy up. Learn the difference between leaving a shell and leaving your workspace running.
concept: Typing exit ends the current shell and closes its pane. Killing a pane also ends programs inside it — so only use these test shells.
steps: Select practice. If a pane is zoomed, unzoom it first.
In each extra pane, type exit and press Enter. Leave exactly one pane in practice.
Keep the last practice shell running.
tip: Detach keeps programs alive; exit ends a shell. They are not interchangeable.
checkpoint: practice still exists with exactly one pane.

title: Travel light
intro: A window closes when its last pane exits. Let's retire the journal without disturbing your home port.
concept: You can close panes individually, or kill an entire window. Always check which window you're in before closing it.
steps: Select journal in the window chooser.
Type exit in its shell. If you added extra panes there, exit those too.
Confirm you're back in practice and it still has a working shell.
tip: Don't practice destructive shortcuts in windows with real work. This dedicated tmux session is for experiments.
checkpoint: journal is gone and practice still exists.

title: Look back over the wake
intro: Output scrolled away? tmux keeps a history you can explore without rerunning the command.
concept: Copy mode lets you navigate tmux’s scrollback while your shell remains running. This lesson uses the standard emacs-style copy-mode keys, set by the trainer for consistency.
steps: Select practice and generate some harmless output: i=1; while [ "$i" -le 80 ]; do echo "Captain Pane log $i"; i=$((i+1)); done
Press Ctrl-b [ to enter copy mode. Use Up or Page Up (Fn-Up on many Mac keyboards) to look through earlier lines.
Press q to return to the live shell. Enter copy mode once more, then click Check my work while still in copy mode.
After passing, click the terminal and press q before beginning the detach mission.
tip: Copy mode and the macOS clipboard are different things. This mission practices scrollback navigation, not system-clipboard integration.
checkpoint: A pane in practice is currently in tmux copy mode.

title: Leave. Return. Carry on.
intro: This is the superpower: your terminal workspace can outlive the terminal looking at it.
concept: Detaching disconnects the display, not the session. The app will keep your tmux server running when you close it, too. A reboot still ends those processes.
steps: If you are still in copy mode, press q first. In practice, run export CAPTAIN_PANE=ahoy to leave a little marker in your shell.
Press Ctrl-b d. The terminal will disconnect, but your shells will keep running.
Click Reconnect terminal, then run echo $CAPTAIN_PANE. Seeing ahoy means you're in the same shell. Now check your work.
tip: You must detach using the keyboard and reconnect for this checkpoint. Closing a shell with exit is not detaching.
checkpoint: Detach from the terminal, then reconnect to the same session.
